techniques.name: RuleFit
techniques.description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A telecoms analytics team fits RuleFit to the predictions of its gradient-boosted churn model rather than to the churn labels, to get a short list of rules that approximates the model. Marketing staff read the top rules, and the team reports how closely the rules reproduce the model's predictions before anyone relies on them.

A lender replaces an opaque default-risk model with a RuleFit model fitted to repayment outcomes. For one declined application, the importance scores show which few rules and income or debt terms drove its score, and the validation team checks them against credit policy.

A hospital team builds an admission-risk model as a RuleFit model fitted directly to patient outcomes, so that clinicians and the ethics committee can read the whole model, a few rules such as 'IF systolic_bp > 140 AND diabetes = true' plus a handful of weights. The team counts the active rules first and keeps the model only if it is short enough to read.

limitations.description: The lasso can leave many rules active, and a model with hundreds of active terms is no longer readable. Rules also approximate smooth linear trends poorly and need many pieces to do so. Count the non-zero terms before calling the model interpretable.

Rules overlap and are often correlated, so a rule's weight cannot be read on its own. 'Temperature above 15' is also true wherever 'temperature above 10' is. With correlated inputs, rules can also suggest interactions that are not in the real relationship.

Tree size sets how long rules can be and which interactions can appear. Shallow trees give short, readable rules but miss high-order interactions, and deep trees capture them at the cost of long rules. No single depth suits every problem.

Fitted to a black-box model's predictions, RuleFit only approximates that model. Without a fidelity check, such as agreement on held-out inputs, its rules describe the surrogate and may not describe the model they are meant to explain.

resources.title: Predictive learning via rule ensembles
resources.abstract: General regression and classification models are constructed as linear combinations of simple rules derived from the data. Each rule consists of a conjunction of a small number of simple statements concerning the values of individual input variables. These rule ensembles are shown to produce predictive accuracy comparable to the best methods. However, their principal advantage lies in interpretation. Because of its simple form, each rule is easy to understand, as is its influence on individual predictions, selected subsets of predictions, or globally over the entire space of joint input variable values. Similarly, the degree of relevance of the respective input variables can be assessed globally, locally in different regions of the input space, or at individual prediction points. Techniques are presented for automatically identifying those variables that are involved in interactions with other variables, the strength and degree of those interactions, as well as the identities of the other variables with which they interact. Graphical representations are used to visualize both main and interaction effects.

resources.title: RuleFit-Based Nomogram Using Inflammatory Indicators for Predicting Survival in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, a Bi-Center Study
resources.abstract: Purpose: Traditional prognostic studies utilized different cut-off values, without evaluating potential information contained in inflammation-related hematological indicators. Using the interpretable machine-learning algorithm RuleFit, this study aimed to explore valuable inflammatory rules reflecting prognosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patients. Patients and Methods: In total, 1706 biopsy-proven NPC patients treated in two independent hospitals (1320 and 386) between January 2010 and March 2014 were included. RuleFit was used to develop risk-predictive rules using hematological indicators with no distributive difference between the two centers. Time-event-dependent hematological rules were further selected by stepwise multivariate Cox analysis. Combining high-efficiency hematological rules and clinical predictors, a final model was established. Models based on other algorithms (AutoML, Lasso) and clinical predictors were built for comparison, as well as a reported nomogram. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and concordance index (C-index) were used to verify the predictive precision of different models. A site-based app was established for convenience. Results: RuleFit identified 22 combined baseline hematological rules, achieving AUROCs of 0.69 and 0.64 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. By contrast, the AUROCs of the optimal contrast model based on AutoML were 1.00 and 0.58. For overall survival, the final model had a much higher C-index than the base model using TN staging in two cohorts (0.769 vs 0.717, P < 0.001; 0.752 vs 0.688, P < 0.001), and showing great generalizability in training and validation cohorts. The two models based on RuleFit rules performed best, compared with other models. As for other endpoints, the final model showed a similar trend. Kaplan–Meier curve exhibited 22.9% (390/1706) patients were “misclassified” by AJCC staging, but the final model could assess risk classification accurately. Conclusion: The proposed final models based on inflammation-related rules based on RuleFit showed significantly elevated predictive performance.

sample_claims.text: The credit risk model's decision logic is expressible as a sparse set of interpretable if-then rules combined with linear feature weights
The patient risk score can be reconstructed from its intercept, active clinical-input rules and linear terms using the recorded clipping and weights.
The fraud detection model identifies risk through comprehensible rules that stakeholders can validate against domain knowledge
The churn-score approximation exposes its weighted rules and linear terms, with agreement assessed against the original model on the stated dataset.

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance, and its accuracy is within the agreed margin of the unconstrained model.
The default-risk model's false-positive and false-negative rates differ between age bands by no more than the agreed tolerance on held-out data.
The COVID-19 screening model's error rates are similar across ethnic groups in each external hospital cohort, with negative predictive value above the clinical threshold set for screening.
Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning trains one shared model across several parties, such as phones or hospitals, without collecting their data in one place. Each party trains the current model on its own data and sends back only an update, such as the changed weights (the model's internal numbers) or the gradients (the direction of change). A central coordinator combines the updates, typically by averaging, into an improved shared model and sends it out again, and the cycle repeats over many rounds. Raw records stay with their owners, which limits how much sensitive data is stored or moved and can support data protection rules that favour collecting less. It is not a privacy guarantee on its own, because updates can still reveal information about the data behind them and the coordinator has to be trusted.

example_use_cases.description: A mobile keyboard team trains a next-word prediction model on users' phones and receives only model updates, so typed text never reaches its servers. The team uses this to decide whether personalised suggestions can ship without collecting message content centrally.

Hospitals in several countries train a model that predicts COVID-19 outcomes on their own patient records and share only model updates with a coordinating centre, so no patient record leaves a hospital. Each hospital's data governance board uses this to decide whether it can join the collaboration.

Several banks jointly train a fraud-detection model on their own transaction data and share only model updates, so no bank's customer records reach a competitor. Each bank's compliance team uses the setup to decide whether joint training fits its data-sharing restrictions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.

A faulty or malicious participant can submit harmful updates that the coordinator cannot check against the participant's data, for example to plant a hidden backdoor in the shared model. Defences such as robust aggregation add cost, and the coordinator must also be trusted with the updates it receives.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

resources.title: Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers
Each participating bank trained the shared fraud-detection model without moving customer transaction records out of its own environment; only model updates reached the coordinator
The central server holds no copy of any participant's raw training data; it holds the shared model and, briefly, the updates it is aggregating

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

resources.title: Using quantile regression to extend an existing wind power forecasting system with probabilistic forecasts
resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

Uncertainty-aware body composition analysis with deep regression ensembles on UK Biobank MRI
resources.abstract: Along with rich health-related metadata, medical images have been acquired for over 40,000 male and female UK Biobank participants, aged 44-82, since 2014. Phenotypes derived from these images, such as measurements of body composition from MRI, can reveal new links between genetics, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic conditions. In this work, six measurements of body composition and adipose tissues were automatically estimated by image-based, deep regression with ResNet50 neural networks from neck-to-knee body MRI. Despite the potential for high speed and accuracy, these networks produce no output segmentations that could indicate the reliability of individual measurements. The presented experiments therefore examine uncertainty quantification with mean-variance regression and ensembling to estimate individual measurement errors and thereby identify potential outliers, anomalies, and other failure cases automatically. In 10-fold cross-validation on data of about 8500 subjects, mean-variance regression and ensembling showed complementary benefits, reducing the mean absolute error across all predictions by 12%. Both improved the calibration of uncertainties and their ability to identify high prediction errors. With intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) above 0.97, all targets except the liver fat content yielded relative measurement errors below 5%. Testing on another 1000 subjects showed consistent performance, and the method was finally deployed for inference to 30,000 subjects with missing reference values. The results indicate that deep regression ensembles could ultimately provide automated, uncertainty-aware measurements of body composition for more than 120,000 UK Biobank neck-to-knee body MRI that are to be acquired within the coming years.

sample_claims.text: On held-out scans, the imaging model's ensemble uncertainty is higher for cases it gets wrong than for cases it gets right, so scans above the uncertainty threshold can be sent for manual review.
The ensemble's predicted probabilities are calibrated on held-out data, so that predictions made with 90% confidence are correct about 90% of the time.
When shown inputs from a class absent from the training data, the ensemble's disagreement is measurably higher than on in-distribution inputs, as tested on a held-out set of unseen-class examples.

The driving system reports an uncertainty level with each detection, derived from disagreement between independently trained networks, and remote operators are alerted when it passes the documented limit.
Each credit score shown to underwriters carries an uncertainty range from the ensemble, and scores with a wide range are labelled as low-confidence.

techniques.name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
techniques.description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. It provides a centralised repository for comparing different experimental runs, reproducing results, and managing model versions. Teams can track hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, model files, and execution environment details, creating a comprehensive audit trail that supports collaboration, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance across the entire machine learning development process.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical diagnosis model experiments across different hospitals, logging hyperparameters, performance metrics, and model artifacts to ensure reproducible research and enable regulatory audits of model development processes.

Managing fraud detection model versions in production, tracking which specific model configuration and training data version is deployed, enabling quick rollback and performance comparison when system reliability issues arise.

Documenting loan approval model experiments with complete parameter tracking and performance logging across demographic groups, supporting fair lending compliance by providing transparent records of model development and validation processes.

limitations.description: Requires teams to adopt disciplined logging practices and may introduce overhead to development workflows if not properly integrated into existing processes.
Storage costs can grow substantially with extensive artifact logging, especially for large models or high-frequency experimentation.
Tracking quality depends on developers consistently logging relevant information, with incomplete logging leading to gaps in experimental records.
Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively.
Security and access control configurations require careful setup to protect sensitive model information and experimental data in shared environments.

resources.title: mlflow
resources.abstract: The open source developer platform to build AI agents and models with confidence. Enhance your AI applications with end-to-end tracking, observability, and evaluations, all in one integrated platform.

resources.title: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow
resources.abstract: Machine learning development creates multiple new challenges that are not present in a traditional software development lifecycle. These include keeping track of the myriad inputs to an ML application (e.g., data versions, code and tuning parameters), reproducing results, and production deployment. In this paper, we summarize these challenges from our experience with Databricks customers, and describe MLflow, an open source platform we recently launched to streamline the machine learning lifecycle. MLflow covers three key challenges: experimentation, reproducibility, and model deployment, using generic APIs that work with any ML library, algorithm and programming language. The project has a rapidly growing open source community, with over 50 contributors since its launch in June 2018.

resources.title: An MLOps Framework for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection with MLflow
resources.abstract: The surge in network traffic has required advanced techniques to ensure network security. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs), which increasingly employ Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methodologies, play a pivotal role in this task by continuously monitoring network traffic patterns and identifying suspicious activities. To address the complexities of developing ML- and DL-based NIDS, MLOps tools have been designed to optimize model deployment, monitoring, and management in production environments, streamlining model development. These tools enable efficient experimentation, version management, and logging of artifacts for network administrators and data scientists. In this work, we design a framework powered by MLflow to manage the ML pipeline from data handling to results visualization. To show the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted an experimental campaign on 4 broadly used security datasets (viz. NSL-KDD, IoT-23, Kitsune, and TON_IoT) performing crucial tasks for intrusion detection, namely anomaly detection, binary misuse detection, and multiclass misuse detection.

resources.title: Enhancing Quantum Software Development Process with Experiment Tracking
resources.abstract: As quantum computing advances from theoretical promise to experimental reality, the need for rigorous experiment tracking becomes critical. Drawing inspiration from best practices in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), we argue that reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in quantum research can benefit significantly from structured tracking workflows. This paper explores the application of MLflow in quantum research, illustrating how it enables better development practices, experiment reproducibility, decision making, and cross-domain integration in an increasingly hybrid classical-quantum landscape.

sample_claims.text: All experimental configurations and hyperparameters tested during model development are centrally logged with their corresponding performance outcomes
The deployed clinical model is reproducible from logged training parameters, data versions, and execution environment specifications
The fraud detection model's performance evolution across successive training runs is traceable through logged metrics and artifact histories
The production model version can be systematically compared against alternative experimental configurations evaluated during development
Model training artifacts and evaluation metrics are accessible to authorized team members through a centralized repository supporting collaborative review

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

resources.title: mgcv: Mixed GAM Computation Vehicle with Automatic Smoothness Estimation
Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Prejudice Remover Regulariser
techniques.description: The Prejudice Remover Regulariser, proposed by Kamishima and colleagues (2012), trains a classifier with an extra fairness penalty that discourages its predictions from carrying information about a sensitive attribute such as gender or race. The penalty approximates the 'mutual information' between the predicted label and the sensitive attribute, which measures how much knowing one tells you about the other. It is added to the usual training objective, so the model is pushed to fit the labels while keeping that dependence low. The authors built it into logistic regression and describe it as applicable to other classifiers that output probabilities. One parameter sets the penalty strength, so a practitioner can trade some accuracy for a smaller dependence on the sensitive attribute.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's modelling team retrains its logistic-regression credit-scoring model with the prejudice remover penalty, using applicant gender as the sensitive attribute. It tries several penalty strengths and records how far approval decisions still depend on gender and how much predictive accuracy is lost at each, so the credit committee can choose the strength it will accept.

A health-system analytics team building a postpartum depression risk model on insurance claims trains it with the penalty, with race as the sensitive attribute. It compares disparate impact and equal opportunity difference with an unpenalised model on the same held-out data, to decide whether the penalised model is good enough or another bias-reduction method is needed.

A university building a model to flag students for early support trains it with the penalty so that flags depend less on gender. The team reports to the student-support board how much accuracy the chosen strength costs, and how far the difference in flag rates between genders shrinks, before the model is used.

limitations.description: The penalty strength has to be tuned, and no setting is right in advance. In the original experiments on census income data, the strongest penalty tested cut the difference in positive-prediction rates between men and women from 0.19 to 0.01, but accuracy fell from about 85% to 77%. The choice is a judgement about how much accuracy to give up.

The sensitive attribute is an input to the model at training and at prediction time, in the original method and in the AIF360 implementation. The technique cannot be used where the attribute is not collected or cannot be used when decisions are made.

The penalty measures only how much predictions depend on the sensitive attribute, not whether errors fall evenly across groups. Where groups really differ in outcome rates in the data, pushing the dependence down misclassifies some individuals to meet the target, and no equal-error-rate guarantee follows.

The original method and the AIF360 implementation cover logistic regression only. Using the penalty with a neural network or another model means deriving and implementing it yourself, and the optimisation was designed for the logistic form.

Reduced dependence is measured on the training sample. With little data, the model can depend on the sensitive attribute more on new cases than on the training data, which the original paper calls underestimation, so the dependence should be re-measured on held-out data.

Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

sample_claims.text: On held-out applications, the mutual information between the credit model's approval decisions and applicant gender is lower than for an otherwise identical unpenalised model, at a penalty strength chosen with its accuracy cost documented.
The gap in shortlisting rates between men and women on held-out data is below the agreed tolerance, with the penalty strength and the accuracy given up at that setting reported.
The postpartum depression risk model's disparate impact ratio between racial groups is closer to 1 than that of the unpenalised model on the same held-out data.

The student-support flagging model's flag rates differ less between genders than those of the unpenalised baseline on held-out students, and the accuracy lost is reported to the student-support board.

techniques.name: Meta Fair Classifier
techniques.description: The meta fair classifier is a general-purpose training algorithm for fair classification. The user chooses a fairness metric, such as the statistical rate (each group's share of favourable outcomes) or the false discovery rate (the share of positive predictions that are wrong), and a target between 0 and 1 for how close to equal the groups' values must be. From labelled training examples that include the protected attribute, the algorithm fits a model of the data, solves a series of constrained optimisation problems, and returns the most accurate classifier that meets the target. It trains a new classifier rather than adjusting an existing one. The original paper proves the result comes close to the best classifier that meets the target, up to the error in the fitted model of the data.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment platform trains a shortlisting classifier with a statistical-rate target of 0.8, so that the selection rate for any gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate, and measures how much accuracy it gives up to reach that target.

A probation service building a recidivism risk classifier constrains false discovery rate parity, so that among people flagged as high risk, the share who do not go on to reoffend is similar across racial groups.

A hospital building a classifier for heart conditions constrains false discovery rate parity, so that false alarms, which send people for unnecessary medical attention, do not fall more heavily on women than on men.

limitations.description: It is a self-contained learner, not a wrapper. It cannot adjust a model you already run, and the paper lists extension to other classifier types as future work. It also needs the protected attribute for every training example, and teams must be willing to replace their model with the one it produces.

The AIF360 implementation supports only statistical rate and false discovery rate, and raises an error for any other metric. The paper's framework covers more, but other criteria, such as equalised odds, mean extra implementation work or choosing a different technique.

The guarantee depends on how well the fitted model of the data matches the real distribution, and the paper's bound carries error terms for any mismatch. In its experiments, a simple fitted model gave lower accuracy than competing methods at the same fairness level.
Results can vary from run to run. In a credit-scoring comparison, repeated runs sometimes missed the fairness target, which made averaging the results unusable.

The method solves a separate constrained optimisation problem for each value on a grid set by the tolerance, and the number multiplies for each additional fairness metric constrained at once. Combining several criteria quickly makes training slow.

resources.title: Classification with Fairness Constraints
resources.abstract: Developing classification algorithms that are fair with respect to sensitive attributes of the data is an important problem due to the increased deployment of classification algorithms in societal contexts. Several recent works have focused on studying classification with respect to specific fairness metrics, modeled the corresponding fair classification problem as constrained optimization problems, and developed tailored algorithms to solve them. Despite this, there still remain important metrics for which there are no fair classifiers with theoretical guarantees; primarily because the resulting optimization problem is non-convex. The main contribution of this paper is a meta-algorithm for classification that can take as input a general class of fairness constraints with respect to multiple non-disjoint and multi-valued sensitive attributes, and which comes with provable guarantees. In particular, our algorithm can handle non-convex "linear fractional" constraints (which includes fairness constraints such as predictive parity) for which no prior algorithm was known. Key to our results is an algorithm for a family of classification problems with convex constraints along with a reduction from classification problems with linear fractional constraints to this family. Empirically, we observe that our algorithm is fast, can achieve near-perfect fairness with respect to various fairness metrics, and the loss in accuracy due to the imposed fairness constraints is often small.

resources.title: Algorithmic decision making methods for fair credit scoring
resources.abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning in evaluating the creditworthiness of loan applicants has been demonstrated for a long time. However, there is concern that the use of automated decision-making processes may result in unequal treatment of groups or individuals, potentially leading to discriminatory outcomes. This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. Through our analysis, we have identified the challenges associated with achieving fairness while maintaining accuracy and profitabiliy, and have highlighted both the most successful and least successful mitigation methods. Ultimately, our research serves to bridge the gap between experimental machine learning and its practical applications in the finance industry.

Among people the recidivism model flags as high risk, the share who do not reoffend differs between racial groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.

techniques.name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
techniques.description: Exponentiated gradient reduction trains a classifier that satisfies a chosen fairness criterion, such as demographic parity (equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups) or equalised odds (equal error rates across groups), while keeping error as low as it can. It reduces the problem to a series of ordinary training runs on the same data, each with different example weights. Between runs, a multiplicative update, the exponentiated gradient step, increases the weight on fairness constraints that are currently violated, and a standard classifier is retrained on the reweighted data. The output is a randomised classifier, a weighted mix of the classifiers trained along the way, with one drawn at random for each prediction. The original paper proves that its error and its fairness violation come close to the best achievable, up to a tolerance the user sets and the statistical error from a finite training set.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment team trains a shortlisting model under a demographic parity constraint so that selection rates are equal across gender groups, and sweeps the method's tolerance setting to see how much accuracy each step towards equality costs.

A justice agency building a recidivism risk model trains a logistic regression under a demographic parity constraint on race, then compares accuracy and fairness metrics against the unconstrained model on the same data before deciding whether to deploy it.

A lender trying equalised odds, true-positive-rate difference and demographic parity as constraints on its credit-scoring model picks the one that gives the best balance of accuracy and profit on its own data, since the best choice differs between datasets.

limitations.description: The guarantees assume the base learner can solve each weighted training problem close to exactly. Real learners only approximate this, so the stated bounds on error and fairness violation are approximate in practice. The learner must also accept per-example weights, which rules out some model types.

The result is a randomised mix of classifiers, so the same input can receive different predictions on repeat requests. This is hard to defend where decisions must be repeatable, as in appeals or audits.

Needs the protected attribute for every training example, although not at prediction time. It enforces one fairness criterion at a time, and the original paper leaves trading off several criteria as an open problem.

Each round retrains the base model, and the number of rounds needed grows with the square of the inverse of the tolerance, so halving the tolerance roughly quadruples training cost. Large datasets or slow models make tight tolerances expensive.

Constraint violation is controlled only up to sampling error, which is larger for small groups. In one credit-scoring comparison the best-performing constraint differed between datasets, so the right criterion has to be found by experiment on the data in hand.

resources.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
resources.abstract: We present a systematic approach for achieving fairness in a binary classification setting. While we focus on two well-known quantitative definitions of fairness, our approach encompasses many other previously studied definitions as special cases. The key idea is to reduce fair classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems, whose solutions yield a randomized classifier with the lowest (empirical) error subject to the desired constraints. We introduce two reductions that work for any representation of the cost-sensitive classifier and compare favorably to prior baselines on a variety of data sets, while overcoming several of their disadvantages.

resources.title: A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.
The recidivism model's true-positive and false-positive rates differ across racial groups by less than the agreed tolerance, and the accuracy cost against the unconstrained model is reported.

techniques.name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
techniques.description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

resources.title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
resources.abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

resources.title: MEDFAIR: Benchmarking Fairness for Medical Imaging
resources.abstract: A multitude of work has shown that machine learning-based medical diagnosis systems can be biased against certain subgroups of people. This has motivated a growing number of bias mitigation algorithms that aim to address fairness issues in machine learning. However, it is difficult to compare their effectiveness in medical imaging for two reasons. First, there is little consensus on the criteria to assess fairness. Second, existing bias mitigation algorithms are developed under different settings, e.g., datasets, model selection strategies, backbones, and fairness metrics, making a direct comparison and evaluation based on existing results impossible. In this work, we introduce MEDFAIR, a framework to benchmark the fairness of machine learning models for medical imaging. MEDFAIR covers eleven algorithms from various categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Through extensive experiments, we find that the under-studied issue of model selection criterion can have a significant impact on fairness outcomes; while in contrast, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not significantly improve fairness outcomes over empirical risk minimization (ERM) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. We evaluate fairness from various perspectives and make recommendations for different medical application scenarios that require different ethical principles. Our framework provides a reproducible and easy-to-use entry point for the development and evaluation of future bias mitigation algorithms in deep learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

techniques.name: Multi-Accuracy Boosting
techniques.description: Multi-accuracy boosting is a post-processing method that corrects a trained classifier's systematic errors on subgroups of people, without retraining it. It needs only the classifier's predictions and a small labelled validation set. An auditor, usually a simple model such as a ridge regression or a shallow decision tree, learns to predict where the classifier's predictions are consistently too high or too low, which finds overlapping subgroups without anyone naming them in advance. Each round fits a small correction for the worst subgroup, as in boosting, and the loop stops when the auditor can find no subgroup whose average error exceeds a chosen tolerance. The result is multi-accuracy, meaning unbiased predictions on every subgroup the auditor can identify, which is not the same as equal accuracy across groups, and the audit itself reports where the original model failed.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital buys a black-box diagnostic model it cannot retrain. Its data team holds a small labelled sample of local patients and runs the audit, which finds that predictions are systematically too low for older women. The team post-processes the model until no subgroup the auditor can find exceeds the agreed error tolerance, then checks that groups the model already served well did not get worse.

A lender uses a vendor's credit-risk model, and its data holds no sensitive attributes. A risk analyst audits the model on a labelled sample of recent applications with a decision-tree auditor, which finds subgroups defined by ordinary features where the errors concentrate. The correction is applied until those subgroups' average error falls within tolerance.

limitations.description: The guarantee covers only subgroups the auditor can identify from the features. If a group's errors follow a pattern too complex for the auditor, or the features carry little trace of group membership, the audit will pass the model while that group is still poorly served.

Multi-accuracy bounds the average prediction error within each identified subgroup. It does not equalise error rates, so large gaps can remain. In the original paper's face-image test, error after correction was still 12.5% for dark-skinned women against 1.0% for light-skinned women.

It needs a labelled validation sample that represents the population and is large enough for the groups of concern. The guarantee for a subgroup weakens as the subgroup's share of the sample shrinks, so rare groups are protected least.

Corrections are fitted on the small audit sample, so too many rounds or an over-flexible auditor will start fitting noise and can make performance worse on new data. The mcboost documentation says its calibration 'tends to overfit' and suggests a smaller step size or fewer iterations.

The method corrects errors against the labels in the audit sample, so it cannot repair bias already built into those labels, such as past decisions recorded as outcomes. A fairer-looking score then still reproduces the earlier pattern.
