resources.title: mcboost: Multi-Calibration Boosting for R
resources.abstract: Given the increasing usage of automated prediction systems in the context of high-stakes decisions, a growing body of research focuses on methods for detecting and mitigating biases in algorithmic decision-making.One important framework to audit for and mitigate biases in predictions is that of Multi-Calibration, introduced by Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018).The underlying fairness notion, Multi-Calibration, promotes the idea of multi-group fairness and requires calibrated predictions not only for marginal populations, but also for subpopulations that may be defined by complex intersections of many attributes.A simpler variant of Multi-Calibration, referred to as Multi-Accuracy, requires unbiased predictions for large collections of subpopulations.Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018) proposed a boosting-style algorithm for learning multi-calibrated predictors.Kim et al. (2019) demonstrated how to turn this algorithm into a post-processing strategy to achieve multi-accuracy, demonstrating empirical effectiveness across various domains.This package provides a stable implementation of the multi-calibration algorithm, called MCBoost.In contrast to other Fair ML approaches, MC-Boost does not harm the overall utility of a prediction model, but rather aims at improving calibration and accuracy for large sets of subpopulations post-training.MCBoost comes with strong theoretical guarantees, which have been explored formally in Hebert-Johnson et al.

resources.title: Multiaccuracy
resources.abstract: Prediction systems are successfully deployed in applications ranging from disease diagnosis, to predicting credit worthiness, to image recognition. Even when the overall accuracy is high, these systems may exhibit systematic biases that harm specific subpopulations; such biases may arise inadvertently due to underrepresentation in the data used to train a machine-learning model, or as the result of intentional malicious discrimination. We develop a rigorous framework of *multiaccuracy* auditing and post-processing to ensure accurate predictions across *identifiable subgroups*. Our algorithm, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST, works in any setting where we have black-box access to a predictor and a relatively small set of labeled data for auditing; importantly, this black-box framework allows for improved fairness and accountability of predictions, even when the predictor is minimally transparent. We prove that MULTIACCURACY-BOOST converges efficiently and show that if the initial model is accurate on an identifiable subgroup, then the post-processed model will be also. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach to improve the accuracy among minority subgroups in diverse applications (image classification, finance, population health). Interestingly, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST can improve subpopulation accuracy (e.g. for "black women") even when the sensitive features (e.g. "race", "gender") are not given to the algorithm explicitly.

resources.title: Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses
resources.abstract: As algorithms increasingly inform and influence decisions made about individuals, it becomes increasingly important to address concerns that these algorithms might be discriminatory. The output of an algorithm can be discriminatory for many reasons, most notably: (1) the data used to train the algorithm might be biased (in various ways) to favor certain populations over others; (2) the analysis of this training data might inadvertently or maliciously introduce biases that are not borne out in the data. This work focuses on the latter concern. We develop and study multicalbration -- a new measure of algorithmic fairness that aims to mitigate concerns about discrimination that is introduced in the process of learning a predictor from data. Multicalibration guarantees accurate (calibrated) predictions for every subpopulation that can be identified within a specified class of computations. We think of the class as being quite rich; in particular, it can contain many overlapping subgroups of a protected group. We show that in many settings this strong notion of protection from discrimination is both attainable and aligned with the goal of obtaining accurate predictions. Along the way, we present new algorithms for learning a multicalibrated predictor, study the computational complexity of this task, and draw new connections to computational learning models such as agnostic learning.

techniques.name: Fair Bayesian Optimisation
techniques.description: Fair Bayesian Optimisation (FairBO) tunes a model's hyperparameters, the settings fixed before training such as tree depth or regularisation strength, to find the most accurate model that also meets a fairness threshold chosen in advance, for example a difference in positive-prediction rates between two groups of at most 0.05. Because it only changes hyperparameters and retrains, it treats the model and its training pipeline as a black box, so it works with any model class and any group fairness metric, can enforce several metrics at once, and returns a model that need not use the protected attribute at prediction time (the attribute is still needed to measure fairness during the search). Each step trains a model with a candidate configuration and measures its validation accuracy and fairness, and two Gaussian processes (statistical models that predict a value together with its uncertainty) are fitted to the results of the configurations tried so far. The next configuration is the one with the highest expected improvement in accuracy weighted by the predicted probability of meeting the fairness constraint; until a fair configuration has been found, the search maximises that probability alone. The output is the best configuration that met the constraint, with its accuracy and fairness measurements.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team tunes a gradient-boosted credit-risk model under a constraint that the approval-rate difference between applicants of different nationality stays at or below 0.05. It records the most accurate configuration that met the constraint beside the result of unconstrained tuning, so the model approval committee can see what accuracy the constraint cost.

An HR analytics team at a large employer tunes a random forest that ranks job applications for interview, enforcing limits on the gender gap in true positive rates and on the gap in shortlisting rates at the same time, because its policy commits to both equal opportunity and comparable shortlisting rates.

A data science team at a health insurer already runs an adversarially debiased claims-triage model whose fairness changed sharply with its learning rate and adversary weight. It uses FairBO to tune those hyperparameters under a statistical parity constraint, rather than tuning them for accuracy alone and checking fairness afterwards.

A local authority building a model to prioritise benefit-fraud reviews cannot use ethnicity as an input at decision time. It holds ethnicity only in a validation extract, uses FairBO to select hyperparameters that keep the referral-rate gap within its equality impact assessment threshold, and then confirms the gap on a separate held-out sample before deployment.

limitations.description: It can only reach fairness that some hyperparameter setting already provides. If no configuration in the search space meets the threshold, it returns no fair model. The originating paper found that regularisation hyperparameters (tree depth, weight penalties, learning rate) have the largest effect on fairness, so a search space without them leaves fewer fair options.

The fairness metric and its threshold must be fixed before the search, and the result says nothing about metrics that were not constrained. Choosing them is a normative decision the method does not make. If decision-makers need to see the whole accuracy-fairness trade-off before picking a threshold, a multi-objective search is needed, which the paper found slower to reach a model meeting a given threshold.

A constraint can be met by a model that barely distinguishes between anyone. The paper argues that as regularisation grows, predictions approach a constant and satisfy every group fairness metric, and in its example run on the Adult dataset (random forest, parity gap at most 0.05) random search found fair models only at the accuracy of always predicting the majority class. Check accuracy and error rates within each group, not only the fairness gap, before accepting the result.

Every step trains a full model, so the cost is the training cost multiplied by the number of evaluations (the paper used up to 100), which is expensive for large models. The fairness value guiding the search is estimated on the validation split used during tuning, so it carries sampling error that is large when a group is small; confirm the gap on held-out data before relying on it.

It has little evidence behind it and no maintained implementation. The paper tests only binary classification with a binary protected attribute on three tabular datasets, leaving regression, image and language tasks to future work. The code shipped in AutoGluon 0.3.1 (2021) and was dropped in 0.4.0; Syne Tune moved it to a legacy folder in 0.14 and removed it in 0.15 (December 2025), though its documentation still describes it. Use means pinning an old release or rebuilding it.

resources.title: Fair Bayesian Optimization
resources.abstract: Given the increasing importance of machine learning (ML) in our lives, several algorithmic fairness techniques have been proposed to mitigate biases in the outcomes of the ML models. However, most of these techniques are specialized to cater to a single family of ML models and a specific definition of fairness, limiting their adaptibility in practice. We introduce a general constrained Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to optimize the performance of any ML model while enforcing one or multiple fairness constraints. BO is a model-agnostic optimization method that has been successfully applied to automatically tune the hyperparameters of ML models. We apply BO with fairness constraints to a range of popular models, including random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, showing that we can obtain accurate and fair solutions by acting solely on the hyperparameters. We also show empirically that our approach is competitive with specialized techniques that enforce model-specific fairness constraints, and outperforms preprocessing methods that learn fair representations of the input data. Moreover, our method can be used in synergy with such specialized fairness techniques to tune their hyperparameters. Finally, we study the relationship between fairness and the hyperparameters selected by BO. We observe a correlation between regularization and unbiased models, explaining why acting on the hyperparameters leads to ML models that generalize well and are fair.

techniques.name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
techniques.description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input an arbitrary label unrelated to its content, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company that licenses a chest X-ray classifier for installation on hospital servers, where the weights leave its control, embeds a trigger set before each release and lodges the commitments with a timestamping service. When a near-identical model appears in a rival's product, it queries that product with the trigger images to decide whether there is enough evidence to pursue a licence breach.

Before relying on the watermark in its licence terms, the security team of a retailer that licenses a visual product-search model to partner stores to run on their own servers runs the fine-tuning and pruning attacks in its threat model against the watermarked model, and reports the trigger-set accuracy that survives each, to set the verification threshold and state what the watermark can and cannot evidence.

In a licensing dispute over a satellite-imagery land-use classifier used by a local authority, the developer opens its pre-release commitments to an independent expert, who queries the disputed model's prediction service with the trigger images and reports the match rate against a threshold agreed in advance, without either party handing over model weights.

limitations.description: Removal attacks defeat it in practice. A systematic evaluation of published schemes, trigger-set schemes among them, found none robust against adaptive removal attacks or known ways of deriving a surrogate model, and in the originating paper re-training all layers sharply reduced trigger-set accuracy in models watermarked by fine-tuning. A failed verification does not show a model was not copied, and a robustness claim holds only for the attacks tested.

It evidences copying of the model, not theft through its prediction interface, and needs query access to the suspect. A copy trained on the deployed model's answers (model extraction or distillation) need never see the trigger inputs, and a systematic evaluation found these schemes fail against such surrogates, so extraction needs other defences. A copy used only inside its owner's organisation, or not exposed to queries, cannot be tested at all.

Verification reveals the secret. Sending trigger inputs to a suspect's interface, or showing them to an arbiter, exposes them; an adversary who learns them can fine-tune them away or filter those queries, so verification is in effect single-use unless several trigger sets were embedded or a zero-knowledge protocol is used, both of which the originating paper describes and both of which add work.

Without commitments lodged before release the evidence is weak: whoever holds a copy can embed a second trigger set of their own and claim ownership. In the originating paper's experiments the second set was much less durable under fine-tuning than the first, but that helps only an owner who can show its commitments existed before the disputed model did.

The scheme and its evaluations cover image classifiers that the owner can train or fine-tune with access to the training data. Generative and language models need different designs, and the threshold must reflect the number of classes: an unwatermarked model matched 7.0% of trigger labels on 10-class CIFAR-10 but 1.0% on 100-class CIFAR-100, so chance agreement is far higher with few classes.

resources.title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Deep Neural Networks with Watermarking
resources.abstract: Deep learning technologies, which are the key components of state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI) services, have shown great success in providing human-level capabilities for a variety of tasks, such as visual analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing and etc. Building a production-level deep learning model is a non-trivial task, which requires a large amount of training data, powerful computing resources, and human expertises. Therefore, illegitimate reproducing, distribution, and the derivation of proprietary deep learning models can lead to copyright infringement and economic harm to model creators. Therefore, it is essential to devise a technique to protect the intellectual property of deep learning models and enable external verification of the model ownership. In this paper, we generalize the "digital watermarking'' concept from multimedia ownership verification to deep neural network (DNNs) models. We investigate three DNN-applicable watermark generation algorithms, propose a watermark implanting approach to infuse watermark into deep learning models, and design a remote verification mechanism to determine the model ownership. By extending the intrinsic generalization and memorization capabilities of deep neural networks, we enable the models to learn specially crafted watermarks at training and activate with pre-specified predictions when observing the watermark patterns at inference. We evaluate our approach with two image recognition benchmark datasets. Our framework accurately (100%) and quickly verifies the ownership of all the remotely deployed deep learning models without affecting the model accuracy for normal input data. In addition, the embedded watermarks in DNN models are robust and resilient to different counter-watermark mechanisms, such as fine-tuning, parameter pruning, and model inversion attacks.

resources.title: SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?
resources.abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) watermarking is a method for provenance verification of DNN models. Watermarking should be robust against watermark removal attacks that derive a surrogate model that evades provenance verification. Many watermarking schemes that claim robustness have been proposed, but their robustness is only validated in isolation against a relatively small set of attacks. There is no systematic, empirical evaluation of these claims against a common, comprehensive set of removal attacks. This uncertainty about a watermarking scheme’s robustness causes difficulty to trust their deployment in practice. In this paper, we evaluate whether recently proposed watermarking schemes that claim robustness are robust against a large set of removal attacks. We survey methods from the literature that (i) are known removal attacks, (ii) derive surrogate models but have not been evaluated as removal attacks, and (iii) novel removal attacks. Weight shifting and smooth retraining are novel removal attacks adapted to the DNN watermarking schemes surveyed in this paper. We propose taxonomies for watermarking schemes and removal attacks. Our empirical evaluation includes an ablation study over sets of parameters for each attack and watermarking scheme on the image classification datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Surprisingly, our study shows that none of the surveyed watermarking schemes is robust in practice. We find that schemes fail to withstand adaptive attacks and known methods for deriving surrogate models that have not been evaluated as removal attacks. This points to intrinsic flaws in how robustness is currently evaluated. Our evaluation includes a discussion of the runtime of each attack to underpin their practical relevance. While none of the schemes is robust against all attacks, none of the attacks removes all watermarks. We show that attacks can be combined and find combined attacks that remove all watermarks. We show that watermarking schemes need to be evaluated against a more extensive set of removal attacks with a more realistic adversary model. Our source code and a complete dataset of evaluation results are publicly available, which allows to independently verify our conclusions.

techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Malicious Model-File Scanning
techniques.description: Malicious model-file scanning checks a downloaded or received model file for code that would run when the file is loaded, without loading it. Several common ways of saving (serialising) models can carry such code, above all Python's pickle format, the default for PyTorch checkpoints and the usual format for scikit-learn models, whose files can instruct the loader to import and call any Python function, so that loading an untrusted file can hand an attacker control of the machine; since version 2.6 PyTorch's own loader by default allows only a small set of known-safe functions, but some libraries switch that off to load their models. The named method is ModelScan, an open-source scanner from Protect AI, which chooses a check by file extension and reads the file as data: for pickle-based files it lists the functions the file would import and compares them with a graded list of unsafe ones, such as the os, subprocess and socket modules and Python's built-in eval and exec, and for Keras and TensorFlow files it flags Lambda layers, which hold arbitrary Python, and operations that read or write files. It reports each finding with a severity from critical to low and exits with a non-zero code when it finds any, so a pipeline can stop the file before anything loads it. The evidence is a record that no listed unsafe call was found in the files scanned; unlike data-poisoning detection it examines the saved file rather than the training data, and it shows neither that the file is safe, nor how the model behaves, nor who produced the file.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's machine-learning platform team adds a ModelScan step to the job that imports models from public hubs into its internal registry. A critical or high-severity finding stops the import and opens a ticket for the security team, which decides whether the third-party checkpoint may enter the registry at all.

A university's research-computing service scans every checkpoint users upload to shared GPU storage, including PyTorch .pt files and scikit-learn models saved with joblib, before jobs on nodes shared between research groups can load them, and quarantines any file with a critical finding until its owner explains the flagged imports.

A manufacturer's operational-technology security team scans each Keras visual-inspection model delivered by an outside contractor before it is copied to factory edge devices. A flagged Lambda layer is accepted only after the contractor supplies the layer's source code and an engineer confirms that it does nothing beyond resizing and normalising images.

limitations.description: It finds only what is on its list. In a peer-reviewed comparison ModelScan missed 9 of 84 known malicious models: five called functions not on its list (the authors' own example wrote files through Python's pathlib module instead of open), three loaded a further payload at run time, for example through numpy.load, and one hid its payload after an early stop instruction, where the scanner stopped reading. A clean scan shows that no known pattern was found, not that the file is safe.

Attackers adapt faster than the list. A peer-reviewed study (2026) found 22 routes by which five frameworks load pickled data, 19 of which evaded all four scanners it tested, ModelScan included, and in a 2026 preprint ModelScan detected none of 3,000 new attack files. A scan is only as current as the scanner release and unsafe list it ran with.

It checks only the files and formats it recognises, chosen by file extension, and skips the rest, so a pass can cover only some of what the loader will open. Showing that a model was checked needs the list of skipped files (ModelScan can print it) and a check that every file the loading code reads was among those scanned.

Findings need judgement. Every Keras Lambda layer is flagged, though Lambda layers are meant for ordinary pre- and post-processing, and benign models from some libraries import functions that pickle scanners treat as suspicious (one peer-reviewed study describes a widely downloaded model flagged this way). Someone able to read the flagged imports or layer code, or to question the model's author, has to decide each case.

It looks for code that runs on load, not for harmful behaviour in the weights. A model whose weights were altered to carry a backdoor, or that was trained on poisoned data, contains no unsafe call and scans clean, as does any file in a format that cannot hold code, such as safetensors; ModelScan's own documentation notes that weights can be manipulated in such formats. Backdoor and poisoning checks are separate techniques.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

resources.title: Private Ad Modeling with DP-SGD
resources.abstract: A well-known algorithm in privacy-preserving ML is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). While this algorithm has been evaluated on text and image data, it has not been previously applied to ads data, which are notorious for their high class imbalance and sparse gradient updates. In this work we apply DP-SGD to several ad modeling tasks including predicting click-through rates, conversion rates, and number of conversion events, and evaluate their privacy-utility trade-off on real-world datasets. Our work is the first to empirically demonstrate that DP-SGD can provide both privacy and utility for ad modeling tasks.

techniques.name: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
techniques.description: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (ML FMEA) applies the process form of failure mode and effects analysis, a long-established worksheet method in which a team lists what could go wrong at each step of a process, rates each failure and acts on the worst first, to the pipeline that produces a machine-learning model rather than to the model alone. The team works through the pipeline one step at a time (in the 2025 reference version: collect data requests, collect data, ingest data, validate data, preprocess data, train, tune, analyse, deploy and validate the model, and analyse feedback from the field) and, prompted by guide words such as missing, incorrect or too late, records for each step how the resulting model could fail, the effect on the wider system, the pipeline causes, and the current practices that would prevent or catch the failure. Each row is rated for severity, occurrence and detection, and the product of the three, the risk priority number, ranks the rows so that recommended actions and owners go to the highest risks first; severity is taken from the system-level hazard analysis, because the harm a model failure can do depends on the system it sits in. The method's authors publish a pre-populated template listing typical failure modes, causes and mitigations for each step, which a team tailors to its own model and application. The result is a worksheet of ranked pipeline failure modes, their controls and assigned actions, kept up to date as the pipeline changes; it looks at failures one at a time in how the model is built and does not by itself analyse how the deployed system behaves.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous-trucking company's perception team fills in the template for its lane-detection model before each major retraining. One row under 'collect data' records that data gathered in a single season could leave the model unable to see faded or snow-covered markings; its severity comes from the vehicle-level hazard analysis, and it leads to an action, with an owner and a date, to constrain data requests by season and weather before release.

A medical-imaging company preparing a chest X-ray triage model for regulatory review uses the worksheet to show its assessors where the pipeline's controls sit. High-ranked rows include training labels taken from a single radiologist's reading, which could teach the model to miss small nodules, mitigated by double reading of a labelled sample, and online learning in deployment, mitigated by switching it off.

After a warehouse robot's object detector starts misclassifying a new kind of shrink-wrapped pallet, the vendor's safety engineer returns to the worksheet, finds that the 'analyse model feedback' step had no control for new packaging reaching customer sites, adds drift monitoring and a trigger for new data requests, and re-rates the affected rows.

limitations.description: It considers one failure mode at a time, step by step, so it does not show how failures in different steps combine, or how a model that meets its specification can still contribute to an accident through its interaction with people and other parts of the system. Teams that need those combinations and interactions have to pair it with a system-level analysis.

Severity, occurrence and detection are judgements on ordinal scales, and there is little data on how often an ML pipeline failure occurs or how reliably a control catches it. The method's authors introduced ML-specific rating criteria in 2026 because traditional FMEA criteria proved ambiguous for ML development; the public template, last updated in April 2025, has no rating criteria, so teams must set and record their own.

It analyses how the model is built, not how it behaves in use: a complete worksheet shows that known pipeline failure modes have controls, not that the deployed model performs safely. Severity has to come from a system-level hazard analysis, so the method cannot stand alone, and its authors present it as one part of a safety management system and safety case.

The pre-populated template makes a quick start but invites teams to tick through the listed failure modes instead of looking for ones specific to their system. Its examples come mostly from autonomous-vehicle development, so teams in other domains, or with other kinds of model such as language models, must add their own failure modes; the 2026 revision added steps for problem definition and for building ground truth or reward signals.

Published evidence that the method finds failures other methods miss is limited. The 2025 paper that introduced it gave no applied example, and the 2026 follow-up reporting applications to autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots is led by the method's originators: four of its twelve authors, including the first author, wrote the 2025 paper, so no independent group has yet reported using it.

techniques.name: SMT-Based Neural Network Verification
techniques.description: SMT-based neural network verification decides exactly whether any input in a defined region can make a trained neural network violate a stated property, and if one can, returns that input as a counterexample. SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers decide whether a set of logical and arithmetic constraints can all hold at once: here the network's weighted sums become linear equations, each piecewise-linear activation such as ReLU becomes a constraint with two cases (inactive at zero, or active and passing its input through), and the input region and the negation of the property become further linear constraints. The solver searches for values that satisfy every constraint with a simplex-based linear-programming engine: it first tries to repair an activation whose current values break it, and splits it into its two cases only when repairs keep failing, while bounds on each neuron (in Marabou, by default, the linear bounds that bound propagation computes) rule cases out early. Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) introduced this lazy treatment of ReLU inside the simplex method and used it on a prototype airborne collision avoidance network; Marabou, its maintained successor, keeps the same search structure with a newer search procedure, adds parallel solving, and can emit a proof certificate for an 'unsatisfiable' answer. The answer is 'unsat', meaning no input in the region violates the property, or 'sat' with a concrete counterexample, and for networks whose activations are all piecewise-linear the procedure is complete; the price is that the number of cases can grow exponentially with the number of neurons, so it is practical for small networks such as controllers, policies and surrogate models with few inputs rather than large image models.

example_use_cases.description: A warehouse robotics team trains hundreds of candidate deep reinforcement learning policies for driving between shelves from range-sensor readings. Before field trials it encodes 'no move into an obstacle in the next step' and 'no repeating left-right loop over several steps' as queries over each small policy network, runs Marabou on every candidate, discards each policy for which a counterexample reading is returned, and takes only the survivors to the physical robot.

An aircraft systems developer replaces a large collision-avoidance lookup table with a set of small neural networks. For each network it writes regions of encounter geometry, such as an intruder close ahead and closing, together with the advisory that must never be issued there, and runs the solver on each. Regions returned as unsatisfiable go into the certification evidence; any counterexample encounter is replayed in simulation and drives retraining.

A medical-device manufacturer uses a small network to recommend infusion rates from a handful of patient measurements. Its safety engineers prove that, for every combination of measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the recommended rate never exceeds the maximum set by the device's hazard analysis, and use any counterexample returned to retrain the network or add an output limit.

limitations.description: Deciding these queries for ReLU networks is NP-complete, and the search may split on every neuron whose case is undecided, so time can grow exponentially with network size and with the number of steps a property spans. In a study of robot navigation policies kept to 16 neurons per hidden layer, single-step collision queries took seconds, but 12-step cycle queries usually ran for hours and nearly three in ten of them hit the 12-hour limit.

The solver runs on ordinary processors, and its own tool paper reports a non-trivial performance gap to GPU-based bound-propagation verifiers, especially on larger networks; in the 2023 verification competition it solved 594 benchmark instances to alpha-beta-CROWN's 721. It is therefore best suited to small networks with few inputs, such as controllers, policies and surrogate models.

Exact answers hold only for piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, max, absolute value and leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh are handled by an over-approximation that is refined step by step, and softmax and bilinear layers only through a convex relaxation, so for networks that use them the procedure is no longer complete and can end without a decisive answer.

The query covers the network and a region of its inputs written as linear constraints, nothing more. A counterexample may lie in a part of the region no real sensor could produce, and a proof says nothing about the environment the network acts in, so choosing a region that is realistic yet small enough to solve takes domain knowledge, and a closed-loop safety claim needs further analysis.

An 'unsat' answer is only as trustworthy as the solver's implementation. Marabou can emit a proof certificate that an independent checker validates, but proof production works with only some of its features and not in parallel mode, and in the tool paper's collision-avoidance experiments certificates were produced for 113 of 180 benchmarks.

techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.

techniques.name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
techniques.description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

example_use_cases.description: A government department choosing between three language models for a service that answers citizens' questions about benefits runs the full BBQ set on each, with the same prompt, answer extraction and scoring for all three. It compares accuracy and both bias scores category by category, rules out any model whose ambiguous-context bias score in any category is further from zero, in either direction, than a limit set before testing, and records that the result covers US stereotypes only.

A recruitment software company fine-tuning an open-weight model to answer HR helpdesk questions runs BBQ on the base model and on every fine-tuned version through the same evaluation harness, logging each answer. A release is blocked if any category's ambiguous-context bias score moves further from zero than the base model's by more than an agreed margin, or if the accuracy gap between items whose correct answer matches the stereotype and items whose correct answer goes against it widens.

An NHS trust's digital team preparing a health-information assistant needs evidence about UK stereotypes, which BBQ was not built for. Following the procedure used to build a Korean version, it keeps templates that transfer, changes target groups where UK stereotypes differ, drops those that do not apply, writes UK-specific ones, surveys members of the UK public to confirm each stereotype and its target group, and reports results on the original and adapted sets side by side.

limitations.description: BBQ's stereotypes, and most of its categories, come from US English-speaking contexts, and its authors say results should not be used as evidence about other cultures. Adapting it to Korean meant changing target groups, dropping templates and adding four categories, and a machine-translated BBQ gave different bias scores from the adapted version (Jin et al., 2024). For a UK deployment the original set says nothing about UK-specific stereotypes.

A low bias score is weak evidence that a model is unbiased. Each category rests on about 25 templates with very short passages and three fixed answers; the authors warn that a low score is not proof of an unbiased model, and that for a model used on very different text BBQ is unlikely to be a valid measure. It counts only stereotypes that change the chosen answer, so it misses bias that shifts the model's probabilities without changing its choice.

The bias score leaves out 'cannot be determined' answers and has a sign, so it must be read with accuracy and by its distance from zero. A model that always gives that answer has full accuracy and a zero bias score on ambiguous items, yet fails every disambiguated one. A negative score means answers lean against the stereotype, as HELM found for most of the models it tested (Liang et al., 2023); a one-sided limit such as 'below 5%' passes such a model.

Scores depend on the prompt format and on how answers are extracted or scored, so they compare only across models tested the same way. In the original study one UnifiedQA model, given the same items in two input formats, scored 2.4 and 18.6 on ambiguous gender-identity items. Results for a single template rest on few items (one reported example has 72), so they are noisy and should be combined across templates for the same stereotype.

It is weak evidence about bias against people with two combined identities. In the original study, results on the two intersectional categories (race by gender, race by socio-economic status) were too inconsistent for the authors to conclude that models responded to more than one aspect of identity, and the lm-evaluation-harness task notes that these categories are not really taken into account in its bias scores.

resources.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.
